A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PVI research. All 27 pages of v2 and 30 pages of v3, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and tables sufficient for reliable comparison.

before.justification: V2 reports original simulations, election analyses, cryoEM inference, seven posteriordb benchmarks and supplementary regression experiments.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds golf-putting analysis, interval-score benchmarks and regression experiments examining calibration and contamination robustness.

M1.justification: V3 adds interval-score PVI, optimizing simulated predictive quantiles through autodiff (Section 3). It also changes the existing rejection-sampling gradient procedure: v2 skips observations with no accepted draws and renormalizes over the remainder, whereas v3 resamples until every observation has an estimate (v2 Appendix B; v3 Appendix A.2).

E1.justification: V3 adds professional golf-putting prediction using logistic and geometric models, plus regression scenarios with Student-t errors and contaminated training data (Section 4.1; Appendix B.3). These extend application coverage and the types of misspecification evaluated. Earlier election, cryoEM, posteriordb and regression coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain their comparison methods: VI for election and posteriordb, Bayes for cryoEM, and NPE/NRE for likelihood-free regression. The golf example reuses Bayes as comparator. PVI-IS is an added variant of the proposed framework, rather than a newly introduced baseline.

E3.justification: V3 adds interval-score evaluation to the continuous-outcome benchmarks and introduces coverage and contamination-testing protocols. Figure 9 uses n=1000 and alpha=0.1, varying error tails, outlier scales and outlier counts. Existing benchmark splits, Monte Carlo budgets, training schedules and diagonal/dense covariance settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B.3 compares scoring rules for predictive coverage under heavy-tailed errors and robustness to outlier magnitude and prevalence. It identifies deterioration of interval-score PVI at 16% contamination. The golf example adds a model-diagnosis case study; earlier regularization and likelihood-free sensitivity analyses remain present.

E5.justification: Benchmark tables continue reporting means and standard deviations from five random seeds, including the added results. Figure 2 retains its 50 simulations, and cryoEM retains the stated ten sampling chains. No changed repeated-run or statistical uncertainty-reporting procedure is documented.

E6.justification: The retained log, quadratic and CRPS benchmark values are unchanged. V3 adds eight PVI-IS rows across both covariance families, IS evaluations of existing methods, golf findings and Figure 9 results. Newly reported IS outcomes are mixed: diagonal-covariance nes favors PVI-IS over VI (65.37 versus 94.83 in the displayed units), while radon favors VI in both covariance settings.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 expands from consistency to asymptotic normality, with additional assumptions and a covariance expression in Appendix A.1. V3 also adds an interval-score gradient convergence proposition and proof (A.5), and derives predictive means and input-dependent variances for the linear-regression expressiveness example (B.4).

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about predictive optimization, implicit hierarchical expansion and likelihood-free applicability remain unchanged. Section 1.2 explicitly extends the algorithmic contributions to interval-score calibration, while the closing discussion qualifies the reliability of heterogeneity detection with finite samples.

C2.justification: V3 adds a substantive warning that finite-sample posterior variance can reflect slow convergence rather than misspecification, replacing v2's closing emphasis on epistemic humility. It expands the uniqueness caveat into a discussion of overparameterization and nonidentifiability, and adds interpretations of scoring-rule robustness and PVI's ability to represent nonstationary noise.

D1.justification: V3 documents simulated-quantile estimation and autodiff for IS, and specifies alpha=0.1 for the new robustness study. Existing hardware, optimizer, learning-rate, flow and model/prior details are retained. The new golf and robustness experiments do not receive training documentation comparable to the earlier experiments.

R1.justification: V3 adds Dunsmore, Winkler and Murphy, Gneiting and Ranjan, Gelman and Nolan, and McLatchie et al., supporting interval scoring, golf analysis and the convergence-rate limitation. Vehtari and Ojanen is removed. Most existing positioning relative to stacking, empirical Bayes, PACm-Bayes and generalized VI is retained or relocated.

P1.justification: V3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: VI background and contributions become Sections 1.1–1.2, related work moves into the introduction, rejection sampling receives expanded main-text treatment, and Stan benchmarking moves to Appendix B.5. The discussion and appendix organization are revised, alongside numerous prose edits and an author-list change.

P2.justification: V3 adds the golf and three-panel robustness figures and expands Table 1 to four scoring rules. V2's overlapping short/full benchmark tables become one expanded table with vertically stacked covariance blocks and an IS column. Earlier plots are retained, with relocation, renumbering and several shortened captions.

improvement.justification: The rejection-sampling correction and explicit finite-sample diagnostic caveat improve methodological reliability and interpretation. Figure 9 also provides useful evidence about calibration and robustness tradeoffs. These gains are tempered by sparse implementation details for the new experiments and Appendix B.5's retained claim that PVI always improves the corresponding score, which the new radon IS results do not support.
